title: Does Scattered Buddha-Recitation Also Lead to Rebirth?
author: Zhanran
excerpt: The Pure Land sutras and treatises all repeatedly teach one to recite the Buddha's name single-mindedly,

inline.s: The Pure Land sutras and treatises all repeatedly teach one to recite the Buddha's name single-mindedly.
How could a Buddhist disciple of decisive faith and earnest vow,
out of fear of difficulty and hardship, defy the teaching of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas by reciting with a scattered mind?
Question: Why should scattered Buddha-recitation not be advocated?

Answer: Because one who recites the Buddha's name with a scattered mind is reciting while indulging in idle thoughts; he cannot achieve right mindfulness at the end of life, and so, following his dying deluded thoughts, he is reborn in the six realms.
Master Shandao taught:
“If a single thought goes astray
(if the one thought at the end of life is not right mindfulness but a deluded thought)
, one will suffer for kalpas
(one will suffer for many kalpas in the round of rebirth in the six realms)
On Right Mindfulness at the Time of Death for Rebirth
) For a discussion of right mindfulness at the end of life, see the article
Right Mindfulness at the End of Life
[Right mindfulness] The thought of Buddha-recitation untainted by deluded thoughts.

Question: But Master Ouyi, in his Exposition on the Nine Grades and Four Lands Through the Recitation of the Name, says: “With decisive faith and earnest vow, even scattered Buddha-recitation necessarily leads to rebirth.”
To this, the following reply is given:
The proposition that “with decisive faith and earnest vow, even scattered Buddha-recitation necessarily leads to rebirth” is mistaken.

The Pure Land sutras and treatises all repeatedly teach one to recite the Buddha's name single-mindedly; how could a Buddhist disciple of decisive faith and earnest vow, out of fear of difficulty and hardship, defy the Buddhas' and bodhisattvas' teaching by reciting with a scattered mind?
Hence Master Ouyi himself, in his Essential Commentary on the Amitabha Sutra, corrected this proposition, clearly stating:
Scattered Buddha-recitation does not guarantee rebirth; only by reciting to the point of single-mindedness is rebirth certain.
The Essential Commentary says:
“Question: Does scattered invocation of the name also remove offenses? Answer: The merit of the name is inconceivable; how could it not remove offenses,
but it does not guarantee rebirth

. For a lax and scattered good deed is hard put to withstand the offenses accumulated since beginningless time. One should know that if accumulated offenses had form and substance, the whole realm of empty space could not contain them; even if for a hundred years, day and night, one recited ten myriad times “Amitabha,” each utterance erasing the births and deaths of eight billion kalpas, the offenses thus erased would be like the soil on a fingernail, and the offenses not yet erased like the soil of the great earth.
Only by reciting to the point of single-mindedness
is one like a vigorous man breaking out through a siege, whom no threefold army can restrain.”
(For details, see
Commentary on the Essential Commentary of the Amitabha Sutra
Moreover, even Master Yinguang, who greatly esteemed Master Ouyi, said:
“With scattered Buddha-recitation, rebirth is hard to attain.”

(From the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang, the letter to the layman Chen Xizhou) None of the other patriarchs ever advocated scattered Buddha-recitation; rather, they censured it. Master Hanshan pointedly observed:
“Reciting ‘Amitabha’ with the mouth while the mind is scattered — shout until your throat bursts, and it is still in vain.”
For details, see
Commentary on the Song of Wasted Effort

With regard to rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, faith, vow, and practice are like the three legs of a tripod — not one can be lacking. Their relationship is this: faith gives rise to vow, and vow guides practice; practice fulfills vow, and practice proves faith. And the proposition that “with decisive faith and earnest vow, even scattered Buddha-recitation necessarily leads to rebirth,” like the views that “faith alone is enough for rebirth” or “faith and vow alone are enough for rebirth,” errs in severing faith, vow, and practice from one another. Hence Master Ouyi, in the Essential Commentary, corrected this severance and gave a comprehensive, profound account of the relationship among the three:
“Faith, vow, and invocation of the name are the essential purport of the sutra. Faith and vow are the practice of wisdom; invocation of the name is the practice of cultivation.”
He also said:
“The practice of wisdom
(faith and vow)
is the guide; the practice of cultivation
(invocation of the name)
is the main practice — like eyes and feet working together.”

Thus faith and vow are like the eyes, invocation of the name like the feet; faith and vow are the guide, invocation of the name the main practice. Master Ouyi also gave a clear teaching on the content and requirements of faith, vow, and practice:

“Faith means faith in oneself and faith in others, faith in cause and faith in effect, faith in the principle and faith in the phenomenal; vow means loathing and renouncing the Sahā world and joyfully seeking the Land of Ultimate Bliss; practice means holding fast to the name,
with single-mindedness
Hence the requirement of practice is: uphold the Name with single-mindedness. And Master Ouyi said:
“Without faith, vow cannot be awakened; without vow, practice cannot be guided; without the wondrous practice of invoking the name
(single-mindedness)
, one's vow cannot be fulfilled nor one's faith realized.”

Thus, if one truly has “decisive faith and earnest vow,” the result must necessarily be single-mindedness. How could scattered Buddha-recitation count as decisive faith and earnest vow? Can one fulfill an earnest vow and realize decisive faith through scattered recitation?

The proposition that “even scattered Buddha-recitation necessarily leads to rebirth” conflicts with the Amitabha Sutra. The Amitabha Sutra teaches that with faith, vow, and invocation of the name to the point of single-mindedness, rebirth is certain. If scattered recitation also necessarily led to rebirth, why would the Buddha speak of single-mindedness (continuous mindfulness without confusion), and why would he repeatedly urge us to “practice as taught”?
In the Praise of the Pure Land, the Buddha's Acceptance and Protection Sutra — Master Xuanzang's translation of the Amitabha Sutra — after the World-Honored One spoke the words,

“If there are good men or good women of pure faith who hear of this Amitāyus Buddha's immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable merit and name, and the adornments of merit of the Land of Ultimate Bliss; having heard, they reflect upon it — for one day and night, or two, or three, or four, or five, or six, or seven,
keeping their thoughts in continuous mindfulness without confusion
(single-mindedness)

. When such good men or good women reach the end of life, Amitāyus Buddha, together with his immeasurable assembly of śrāvaka disciples and bodhisattvas, will surround them and come before them, compassionately protecting and sustaining them so that their minds are not confused. Once they have relinquished this life, they follow the Buddha's assembly and are born in the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitāyus Buddha,”
he immediately said:

“If there are good men or good women of pure faith who hear of this Amitāyus Buddha's inconceivable merit and name, and of the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, all of them should accept it with faith and give rise to the vow,
practicing as taught
, and be born in that Buddha-land.”
In the sutra, the World-Honored One stresses again and again, over and over, the need to
“practice as taught”
. The “practice as taught” spoken of here means that faith, vow, and invocation of the name must reach continuous mindfulness without confusion (single-mindedness). And it tells us clearly:
as long as one practices as taught

, one is received and upheld by the Buddhas of the ten directions, is certain to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, and will never retreat, swiftly realizing Buddhahood — the solicitude in these words overflows. The World-Honored One taught:

“If there are good men or good women of pure faith who hear of this Amitāyus Buddha's inconceivable merit and name, and of the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, all of them should accept it with faith and give rise to the vow,
practicing as taught
, and be born in that Buddha-land.”
Those who practice as taught

, all of them are certain to attain non-retrogression in anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi, and all are certain to be born in the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitāyus Buddha. Therefore, Śāriputra, you and all beings should all accept, receive, and comprehend the words of myself and the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones of the ten directions, and should diligently strive,
practicing as taught
, without giving rise to doubt.”
Those who practice as taught

, all are certain to attain non-retrogression in anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi, and all are certain to be born in the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitāyus Buddha. Therefore, Śāriputra, if there are good men or good women of pure faith, all of them should, toward the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitāyus, have deep faith and understanding, and give rise to the vow to be reborn there,
and not be lax

“In this defiled Sahā world of endurance, in the evil time of the five corruptions, if there are good men or good women of pure faith who hear of this Dharma so hard to believe in all the world, and can give rise to faith and understanding, receiving, upholding, and proclaiming it,
practicing as taught

, know that such a person is extremely rare, having planted good roots before immeasurable Buddhas. At the end of life, such a person is certain to be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, enjoying the Mahāyāna Dharma bliss of the pure Buddha-land adorned with every kind of merit.”

The proposition that “even scattered Buddha-recitation necessarily leads to rebirth” is in fact a denial of the Buddha's teaching of “practicing as taught” in the Praise of the Pure Land, the Buddha's Acceptance and Protection Sutra, and is gravely mistaken.

The proposition that “even scattered Buddha-recitation necessarily leads to rebirth” was repudiated by Master Ouyi himself (the ninth patriarch of the Pure Land school) during his own lifetime. Moreover, before him, no Pure Land patriarch — including Master Shandao and Master Yongming, both said to be emanations of Amitabha Buddha — ever said that scattered recitation necessarily leads to rebirth. And all the Pure Land patriarchs of successive generations after him also clearly opposed this proposition.
Master Jieliu (the tenth patriarch of the Pure Land school) said:

“In seven days of invoking the name, what matters is single-mindedness — uninterrupted and unadulterated — not that the recitation be fast or numerous. … If, however, after the seven days one puts it aside as if unheard, the familiar places never being born in the mind and the unfamiliar places still hard to grow familiar, with the habits of ignorance and karma entwining and entangling, and one merely seeks to earn merit in seven days, yet within those seven days never reaches the state of single-mindedness — this is precisely what is meant by having scant good roots and scant merit and conditions; how can one hope to be reborn in that land?”
(From Starting the Seven-Day Retreat: Address to the Assembly)
Master Xing'an (the eleventh patriarch of the Pure Land school) said:

“If a Buddha-reciter truly attains single-mindedness, the Buddha's mindfulness and protection are not in vain. But if he has not attained single-mindedness, and mistakes light ease for dhyāna, or shallow understanding for deep awakening, then whatever he attains gives rise to arrogance of attainment — this is his own fault, not the Tathāgata's. … If at the end of life a single thought is inverted, not only will he not be born in the nine grades, but he will hardly avoid the three paths; though the Buddha is greatly compassionate, he cannot save me. Alas! Alas!”
(From Distinguishing the Demonic in Buddha-Recitation)
Master Chewu (the twelfth patriarch of the Pure Land school) said:
“Single-mindedness is the destination of the pure karma and the great gate of the Pure Land. If one has not entered this gate, one is never truly secure — how can the student not exert himself!”
He also said:

“In this gate of the Pure Land, with the mind of faith and vow alone, one single-mindedly invokes the name; when one invokes to the point of single-mindedness, the pure karma is thereby greatly accomplished, and rebirth after death is certain.”
(From the Collected Works of Master Chewu)
Master Yinguang (the thirteenth patriarch of the Pure Land school) greatly esteemed Master Ouyi, but with regard to the saying,
“even scattered Buddha-recitation necessarily leads to rebirth,”
Master Yinguang said: “
With scattered Buddha-recitation, rebirth is hard to attain. … With single-minded Buddha-recitation, rebirth is certain.
” (From the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang
, the letter to the layman Chen Xizhou)
Moreover, the patriarchs of the Pure Land school through the ages all clearly taught:
rebirth through right mindfulness at the end of life
(for details, see the article
Right Mindfulness at the End of Life

(If one always recites with a scattered mind in daily life, how can one attain clear right mindfulness at the end of life?) For example, Master Xing'an (the eleventh patriarch of the Pure Land school) said:
If at the end of life a single thought is inverted
, not only will one not be born in the nine grades, but one will hardly avoid the three paths; though the Buddha is greatly compassionate, he cannot save me. Alas! Alas!”

(From Distinguishing the Demonic in Buddha-Recitation) (Translation: If at the end of life a single thought is inverted, not only can one not attain rebirth in the nine grades of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, but one will even find it hard to avoid falling into the three evil paths of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals; though Amitabha Buddha is greatly compassionate, he cannot save me. What is to be done! What is to be done!)

[Three paths] Also written “three paths.” They are the path of fire, the path of blades, and the path of blood, equivalent in meaning to the three evil realms of hell beings, hungry ghosts, and animals — the realms to which one is led by the evil karma of body, speech, and mind. 1. The path of fire: this is the hell realm, where beings are constantly tormented by boiling cauldrons and burning coals, and where fires are many, hence it is called the path of fire. 2. The path of blades: this is the hungry-ghost realm, where beings constantly suffer being driven and pressed by blades and staves, hence it is called the path of blades. 3. The path of blood: this is the animal realm, where the strong subdue the weak and devour one another, drinking blood and eating flesh, hence it is called the path of blood.
But one who recites with a scattered mind cannot achieve right mindfulness at the end of life.
Therefore,
Master Hanshan taught:
“Reciting ‘Amitabha’ with the mouth while the mind is scattered — shout until your throat bursts, and it is still in vain.”
(For details, see
Commentary on the Song of Wasted Effort
Master Ouyi, in the
Vow to Establish a Pure Assembly During Great Illness
written a little over a month before his death, recorded his condition during the illness:
“Now illness besets my body;
though the mind is clear, my strength is not my own

, and I weep and cry out, not knowing what to do. Fortunately, relying on the Buddha's compassion, my fading breath has not yet ceased. If I do not urgently exert myself in the pure karma, how shall I ever escape the wheel of suffering?”
Translation:
Now illness besets my body.
In my heart,
although
I
understand
that I should raise right mindfulness and hold it fast in order to seek rebirth,
yet
my strength is not my own
, I weep and cry out,
at a loss what to do
. Fortunately,
relying
on the Buddha's
compassion
my life
has not ended (had it ended then, the consequences would be unthinkable); if I do not urgently and earnestly cultivate the pure karma
how shall I ever escape the round of birth and death?
Hence Master Ouyi wrote this
Vow to Establish a Pure Assembly During Great Illness
“inviting like-minded Dharma companions (ten persons) and lay protector bodhisattvas and śrāmaṇeras (five persons), with one harmonious mind, to form an assembly for three years
(to form a pure assembly for three years)
in order to recite the Buddha's name diligently and ensure rebirth through right mindfulness at the end of life. (For details, see
Vow to Establish a Pure Assembly During Great Illness

[Crying out] To wail and cry. [Right mindfulness] The right mindfulness of the Pure Land school is the thought of Buddha-recitation untainted by deluded thoughts (thought after thought in succession); the right mindfulness of the Chan school is no-thought (not a single thought arising). [Not knowing what to do] At a loss what to do. “wǎng” means “not”; “yóu” means “where.” [xù] To exert oneself. [Wheel of suffering] The bitter fruit of birth and death revolves without ceasing, hence it is called
wheel
If Master Ouyi had still maintained that “even scattered Buddha-recitation necessarily leads to rebirth,” or that “faith and vow alone suffice for rebirth” (for details, see
Whether One Is Reborn or Not
), how could he, when gravely ill and near death, because of
“though the mind is clear, my strength is not my own,”
have
“wept and cried out, not knowing what to do
(at a loss what to do)
And how could he have repented of his
“neglect of contemplation and practice”
? How could he have needed to hastily establish a pure assembly and diligently recite the Buddha's name in order to seek rebirth? And he further said:
“If I do not urgently exert myself in the pure karma
(if I do not urgently and earnestly cultivate the pure karma)
, how shall I ever escape the wheel of suffering
(how shall I ever escape the round of birth and death)

[Contemplation and practice] To contemplate the principle in the mind and to act in the body in accord with the principle. [Neglect] The same as “huangshu” (desuetude) — to grow rusty through lack of regular practice.
Faith, vow, and practice — these three provisions of the path are the core of Pure Land cultivation. The three are inseparable, and their relationship is:
faith gives rise to vow, and vow guides practice; practice fulfills vow, and practice proves faith.
These sixteen characters are the basic guiding principle of Pure Land cultivation.

That is to say, faith and vow must be realized in practice in order to be genuine faith and earnest vow; and practice is at once the concrete action that realizes faith and fulfills vow, and the yardstick by which the genuineness of faith and the earnestness of vow are measured. A Buddha-reciter must possess genuine faith and earnest vow, and, in accord with the sutra text, practice as taught.

Question: I read an article online that said: “Recently someone told me, in great anxiety and heaviness, that the head of a certain large Buddhist hospice-recitation group in Taiwan was in a very poor state at the end of his life and was not reborn in the West. Also, someone else dejectedly said that a certain master, who had prostrated two million five hundred thousand times to the Buddha, also had a poor end and probably was not reborn in the West either.” How could this be?
Answer: This is because these two people had not clearly understood the conditions for rebirth, and so in their daily practice they did not cultivate in accordance with the conditions for rebirth.
Question: Then what are the conditions for rebirth?
Answer: The condition for rebirth is:
ten consecutive thoughts at the end of life.

This condition for rebirth was taught by Master Shandao, an emanation of Amitabha Buddha, Master Yongming, an emanation of Amitabha Buddha, and the sages who attained realization, Master Tanluan and Master Daochuo;
it is the authoritative word of sages
For details, see
How One Can Attain Rebirth
and
The Conditions for Rebirth: Ten Consecutive Thoughts at the End of Life
[Authoritative word of sages] This is what the sages said; it is correct and free of error, and certain to be trusted and accepted.
Question: There is a view that says: “Even if one recites with a scattered mind, as long as faith and vow are fully present, one will necessarily be reborn.” Is this view correct?
Answer: Both the Buddha and the patriarchs repeatedly taught one to recite the Buddha's name single-mindedly (for details, see the section “single-minded invocation of the name” in
Master Shandao's Teaching of the Pure Land
), and repeatedly exhorted us to practice as taught (for details, see
Commentary on the Praise of the Pure Land, the Buddha's Acceptance and Protection Sutra

). Therefore, one whose faith and vow are fully present is certain to practice as taught and to recite the Buddha's name single-mindedly. One who recites with a scattered mind does so out of fear of difficulty and hardship, thus acting against the teaching of the Buddha and the patriarchs —
this is precisely the concrete manifestation of faith that is not genuine and a vow that is not earnest
Hence one who recites with a scattered mind is certain to lack full faith and vow.

“Even if one recites with a scattered mind, as long as faith and vow are fully present” means: to recite with a scattered mind and yet have full faith and vow. Such a state simply does not exist; it is a pseudo-proposition, just as there is no brave soldier who flinches in the face of battle. Since such a state does not even exist, how can one speak of whether it leads to rebirth or not? Hence “even if one recites with a scattered mind, as long as faith and vow are fully present, one will necessarily be reborn” is fundamentally a fallacy.
[Pseudo-proposition] A proposition that is untrue. [Proposition] A declarative statement expressing a judgment.
With regard to single-minded Buddha-recitation
, Master Shandao, in the Commentary in Four Fascicles on the Contemplation Sutra, taught:
Single-mindedly

invoking the name of Amitabha exclusively — whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, regardless of how long or short the time, thought after thought without relinquishing it — this is called the karma of right concentration,
because it accords with that Buddha's vow

(Translation: To invoke the name of Amitabha Buddha single-mindedly and exclusively — whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, regardless of how long or short the time, thought after thought without relinquishing it — is called the karma of right concentration, because it accords with the vow of Amitabha Buddha.)

[Single-minded] Master Tanluan, in his Commentary on the Treatise on Rebirth, taught: “Single-minded” means thought following thought in succession, without any other thought intervening. (For details, see
Master Tanluan's Teaching of the Pure Land

) [Thought after thought without relinquishing] Every thought is the name of Amitabha. [Right concentration] Correct dhyāna. Body and mind pure and clear, without scattering, is called “right concentration.” [Karma] The activities of body, speech, and mind. [Because it accords with that Buddha's vow] “Single-mindedly invoking the name of Amitabha — whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, regardless of how long or short the time, thought after thought without relinquishing it” — this is because it accords with the vow of Amitabha Buddha.
Master Shandao is an emanation of Amitabha, and his words are the words of Amitabha Buddha. From this we know that for a being to
recite the Buddha's name single-mindedly, thought after thought without relinquishing it
, is to accord with the Buddha's (Amitabha Buddha's) vow. Then,
to recite with a scattered mind is to go against the Buddha's vow!
[Scattered Buddha-recitation] Reciting the Buddha's name with the mouth while the mind thinks of other things.
With regard to scattered Buddha-recitation
Master Hanshan, in the Song of Wasted Effort, taught:
Reciting ‘Amitabha’ with the mouth while the mind is scattered — shout until your throat bursts, and it is still in vain.”
[Song of Wasted Effort] “

“fei” means to spend time and energy; “xian” means useless, wasted effort. “Wasted effort” means spending time and energy without any real result — what is commonly called making futile effort. In the Song of Wasted Effort, Master Hanshan points out the common pitfalls of wasted effort in cultivation, and how to walk out of them.
(For details, see
Commentary on the Song of Wasted Effort
Master Hanshan's teaching is now transcribed and annotated as follows:

To chant the name is easy, but a faithful heart is hard; when mouth and mind are not as one, the labor is all in vain. The mouth recites “Amitabha” while the mind strays far and wide; shout until your throat gives out — still it is all in vain.

Reciting the Buddha's name is easy, but a faithful, sincere heart is hard; when mouth and mind are not at one (the mind not faithful: the mouth recites the Buddha's name while the mind thinks of other things), it is always wasted effort (all is in vain). The mouth recites “Amitabha” while the mind thinks of other things — shout until your throat bursts, and it is still in vain.

[Faith] A faithful, sincere heart; when mouth and mind are not at one, it is false. Hence the next line: “when mouth and mind are not at one, it is always wasted effort (all is in vain).” The “faith” here is not the faith of faith-vow-practice, but the meaning of being faithful and sincere.
For example, the “trade wind” is the wind that arrives on schedule every year when the season comes — the faithful wind.

[Faithful] Honest, not deceptive. [Shout until your throat bursts, and it is still in vain] Because “reciting ‘Amitabha’ with the mouth while the mind is scattered (scattered Buddha-recitation)” cannot accomplish ten consecutive thoughts at the end of life (the minimum requirement for rebirth, for details see
The Conditions for Rebirth
), one does not attain rebirth and the effort is wasted.
Here Master Hanshan pointedly observes:
“Reciting ‘Amitabha’ with the mouth while the mind is scattered
(scattered Buddha-recitation)
, shout until your throat bursts, and it is still in vain.”
